common_name: Candy Hearts Bleeding Heart (Compact Rose-Pink Reblooming Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Terra Nova hybrid resents summer waterlogging more than most bleeding hearts.

directions: Candy Hearts is one of the Terra Nova Nurseries hybrids bred from Dicentra formosa and D. eximia to combine a compact, mounding habit with an extended bloom season. Blue-green, finely dissected foliage stays tidy through summer while arching stems carry clusters of rounded, rose-pink, heart-shaped flowers from spring into fall in cooler climates. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and deadhead spent stems to encourage repeat flowering. It combines well with hostas and ferns as a long-blooming edger for the shaded border.

common_name: Langtrees Bleeding Heart (Blue-Grey Foliage Pacific Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade; established clumps spread steadily by rhizome to form an attractive groundcover.

directions: Named for the Somerset garden where it arose, 'Langtrees' is prized for cool blue-grey, finely cut foliage that pairs handsomely with pale creamy-pink, heart-shaped flowers held above the leaves on arching stems in late spring. Like other Pacific bleeding hearts, it thrives in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and spreads gradually by rhizomes to form a long-lived woodland groundcover. It tolerates summer heat better than the straight species where soil stays moist, though foliage may go summer-dormant in hot climates. Divide congested clumps in early spring or fall to maintain vigor and to propagate more plants true to type.

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall; because named color forms don't come reliably true from seed, propagate by lifting and separating the small tuber offsets that form around the parent tuber after foliage dies down.

directions: Widely regarded as the finest selection of spring fumewort, 'George Baker' produces dense racemes of vivid brick-red to salmon-orange flowers held above finely cut, blue-green foliage in early spring, well before most deciduous trees leaf out. Like the species, it is a true spring ephemeral, completing its growth cycle quickly and dying back to a dormant tuber by early summer, so mark its location and interplant with later-emerging perennials or groundcovers. Plant tubers in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and top-dress with leaf mold to mimic its native woodland habitat. Clumps slowly bulk up over the years as offset tubers form, eventually forming a dense colony.

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall before the ground freezes.

directions: 'Beth Evans' is a vigorous, free-flowering selection of spring fumewort with dense spikes of clear pink flowers held above finely divided, blue-green foliage in early spring. It shares the species' spring-ephemeral habit, emerging, flowering, and setting seed before dying back completely to a dormant tuber by early summer, so interplant it with later perennials to cover the gap it leaves. Plant tubers in fall, about 2-3 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. It self-seeds and slowly forms offset tubers, naturalizing into an increasingly generous drift over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall; flowers slightly earlier than most Corydalis solida forms.

directions: Native to the Caucasus Mountains, Corydalis malkensis is a spring-ephemeral tuberous perennial closely related to C. solida, producing short spikes of pure white, spurred flowers above gray-green, finely divided foliage in very early spring. It flowers slightly ahead of most Corydalis solida forms, often overlapping with snowdrops, and then goes fully dormant by late spring, disappearing until the following year. Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees, where it naturalizes slowly by self-seeding and tuber offsets. Its clean white flowers make an effective contrast planted among the pinks and reds of Corydalis solida cultivars.

common_name: Bressingham Purple Jacob's Ladder (Purple-Flushed Foliage Polemonium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; keep foliage color vivid by avoiding hot, dry sites.

directions: 'Bressingham Purple' is a foliage selection of Jacob's ladder with new growth that emerges deep purple-black before maturing to purple-flushed green, providing season-long color contrast in the shade border even before its clusters of lavender-blue, cup-shaped flowers open in late spring. Purple pigmentation is most intense in cool weather and with morning sun, fading toward green in hot summer conditions. Grow it in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and foliage color. It pairs well with golden-leaved hostas or ferns, whose contrasting color and texture set off the dark young foliage.

common_name: Purple Rain Jacob's Ladder (Purple-Foliage Yezo Polemonium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun.

directions: 'Purple Rain' is a compact selection of the Japanese Jacob's ladder with dusky purple-flushed young foliage that matures to deep green, topped from mid to late spring by loose clusters of sky-blue, bell-shaped flowers with a darker purple eye. Its neat, mounding habit is smaller and tidier than common Jacob's ladder, making it well suited to the front of a shaded border or a woodland rock garden. Grow it in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun which can scorch the purple foliage tones. Divide clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor and to increase stock true to type.

common_name: Blue Pearl Jacob's Ladder (Compact Creeping Polemonium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade.

directions: 'Blue Pearl' is a compact selection of the native creeping Jacob's ladder, forming a low, tidy mound of ladder-like foliage topped in mid-spring with clusters of clear sky-blue, bell-shaped flowers. It shares the species' preference for cool, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil and spreads gently by short rhizomes into a slowly expanding patch rather than running aggressively. Grow it in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees, where it combines well with native ferns, trilliums, and other spring wildflowers. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain compact form and vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow seed in fall or cold-stratify and sow in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acid soil in partial shade; native to moist meadows and open woodlands of the Pacific Northwest, it prefers cool summers and reliable moisture.

directions: Native to moist meadows, streambanks, and open woodlands from the Pacific Northwest to Northern California, Oregon Jacob's ladder produces loose clusters of nodding, salmon-pink to lavender or occasionally white, bell-shaped flowers held above ladder-like compound leaves from late spring into summer. It prefers cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade and performs best where summers stay relatively mild; hot, dry conditions cause early summer dormancy. Direct sow fresh seed in fall, or cold-stratify seed for four to six weeks before an early spring sowing, since germination is more reliable after a cold period. It combines naturally with native ferns, camas, and other Pacific Northwest woodland-edge perennials in a naturalistic planting.

planting.note: Set out dormant crowns or container plants in fall into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade to partial shade; mark the planting spot since the corm-like rootstock disappears completely by early summer.

directions: This pink-flowered selection of Virginia bluebells retains the rosy-pink bud color typical of the species, but the flowers fail to shift to blue as they open, instead remaining a soft, clear pink throughout bloom and creating an unusual color break in a spring shade garden usually dominated by blue. Culture matches the species exactly: rich, consistently moist woodland soil in dappled to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees that leaf out after flowering finishes. The entire plant disappears underground by early summer, so pair it with later-emerging hostas, ferns, or heucheras to fill the gap, and mark clump locations to avoid disturbing the dormant rootstock. Propagate by careful division of dormant crowns in fall, since the pink trait does not reliably come true from seed.

common_name: Dayglow Pink Heucherella (Gold Foliage with Hot Pink Flower Spikes)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; deadhead spent flower spikes to tidy the clump and encourage additional bloom flushes.

directions: Dayglow Pink is grown as much for its abundant, bright pink flower spikes as for its foliage, producing a far heavier bloom than most heucherella cultivars, which typically flower only lightly. Chartreuse-gold, maple-shaped leaves form a tidy mound beneath tall, vivid pink flower spires that rise well above the foliage from late spring into summer. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep roots cool through summer heat. Deadhead spent spikes to maintain a tidy appearance and to encourage additional flushes of bloom over the season.
